newsitem.title: UK: Dlr winces at new highs after flirt with 120 yen.
newsitem.headline: Dlr winces at new highs after flirt with 120 yen.

text.p: The dollar ended the week here shy of new 31-month highs against the mark and well off a fresh 47-month high above 120 yen as uncertainty about the reaction of authorities to the recent dollar rally crept into the market.

The dollar/yen rate suffered severe whiplash in early trading. Japanese government reports that yen weakness would not be detrimental to the economy propelled the dollar as high as 120.15 yen, only to be met immediately with official protests about the yen slide and rumours of Bank of Japan intervention.
Bullishness toward dollar/mark was also tempered by some brisk German inflation data and cautious Bundesbank statements.
Dollar sentiment was subdued later in the session as U.S. stocks extended Thursday's sharp slide, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 75.43 points at 1613 GMT.

"There is growing interest about what the Japanese and German authorities will tolerate in terms of further dollar strength and there may well be an assymetry of views here," said Julian Jessop, economist at Nikko Europe.

Jessop said the Japanese seem happy with a weaker yen but not with excessive volatility, while the Bundesbank may start to grow wary of a weaker mark given the latest inflation data, particularly import price inflation.
At 1621 GMT, the dollar was trading at 118.80/85 yen compared with 119.54/59 yen late Thursday and down almost one-and-a-half yen from the new peak at 120.15 set early in the session.
Against the mark, it was at 1.6255/60 compared with 1.6393/96 late yesterday and down two pfennigs from the 31-month high set earlier in the week.

The dollar/yen's early surge was prompted by a report by Japan's Economic Planning Agency saying that yen weakness was not a negative for the economy. No sooner had it popped above the psychological 120 level, however, than unconfirmed rumours of Bank of Japan dollar sales knocked it back quickly.

Shortly afterwards a Japanese Ministry of Finance official said that "an excessive depreciation of the yen is not welcome" and that the Japanese economy is stronger than the markets currently perceived.

This statement was followed by the Japanese government's chief spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama, who said currency instability is undesirable and he was confident Japan's economic situation is such that the yen will not fall below the 120 yen level.
"I think the Japanese are getting worried about the movement in dollar/yen but can't seem to get their act together to do anyting coherent about it," said Michael Burke at Citibank.

Burke, an economist at Citibank, said the key for investors is still that they are getting paid highly, in terms of the interest rate premium, to hold dollars instead of yen. Economic data out next week would again reinforce expectations of a U.S. interest rate rise, he said.

The concern for dollar bulls, however, is that a consensus to stall the dollar's rally among Japanese authorities may see the Bank of Japan offload some of its massive dollar reserve holdings, which are currently in excess of $200 billion.
A robust rise in German import price inflation in December raised concern about the Bundesbank's dollar/mark view.
German import prices rose a robust 0.8 percent during the month and raised market concern that the recent slide of the mark was responsible and may begin to stoke consumer price inflation too.
"The rise in imported inflation may not yet be a policy making problem but it is certainly not welcome in Frankfurt," said Burke at Citibank.
Bundesbank vice-president Johann-Wilhelm Gaddum further dampened speculation about more interest rate cuts by saying there was no change in the bank's steady monetary policy.
